title: Generative Replay Mitigates Sample Starvation in Quantum Architecture Search
authors: Akash Kundu, Amit Kumar Jaiswal, Sebastian Feld, Prayag Tiwari
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can automate quantum architecture search, but its scalability is limited when useful circuit trajectories become rare in the rapidly expanding search space. Existing replay mechanisms reuse observed transitions; the proposed learned model produces additional predicted one step transitions from real state-action seeds. Here we introduce GenQAS, a tensor network-guided RL framework that combines a fixed matrix product state warm-start with prioritized generative replay. A learned local transition model generates synthetic circuit transitions on demand and mixes them with real experience during Double Deep Q-Network updates. Under a random exploration analysis, near ground state circuits occupy a rapidly shrinking region of the accessible state space. We investigate whether real data anchored synthetic replay can improve the effective training signal in this regime. Across chemical Hamiltonian benchmarks from 6 to 12 qubits, GenQAS improves fixed-budget success probability and identifies compact circuits at competitive energy error. At 12 qubits, it improves final success probability by up to $7.0\times$ over passive replay. On a 15-qubit transverse field Ising model, GenQAS increases success probability from $12\%$ to $21\%$. In a noisy 6-qubit BeH$_2$ transfer experiment, generative replay reduces the steps to chemical accuracy by $92.7\%$. These results show that generative replay can mitigate sample starvation in quantum architecture search and support more resource efficient circuit discovery.
summary: This paper addresses the sample starvation problem in Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) by introducing GenQAS. This method enhances reinforcement learning by using a learned model to generate synthetic, yet physically informed, circuit transitions. The results demonstrate that this generative replay significantly boosts the efficiency and success rate of discovering optimal quantum circuits for chemistry and condensed matter simulations.
main_problem: Reinforcement learning for Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) suffers from sample starvation as the search space grows, making it difficult to find optimal quantum circuits.
main_result: The proposed GenQAS framework significantly improves the success probability of finding low-error quantum circuits across various qubit counts, showing up to a 7.0x improvement at 12 qubits.
method: It introduces GenQAS, a tensor network-guided RL framework that augments standard replay buffers by using a learned local transition model to generate synthetic, on-demand circuit transitions.
model_or_system: The system involves constructing parameterized quantum circuits (PQC) to approximate the ground state of chemical Hamiltonians (e.g., $	ext{BeH}_2$, transverse field Ising model) using qubits.
key_observables: Success probability, energy error, and the useful-transition density ($ho$).
important_parameters: Qubit count (6 to 15), generation ratio ($G_r$), and the depth of the circuit.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the synthetic transitions generated by the learned model remain sufficiently consistent with the real environment to support stable off-policy learning.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how GenQAS converts passive replay into active experience generation, showing the limitations of passive replay versus the enhanced training signal from generative replay.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the sample starvation problem in QAS, then details the GenQAS methodology combining MPS warm-starts with generative replay, and finally presents quantitative results across multiple chemical and Ising model benchmarks.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, scalable ML technique to overcome fundamental data scarcity issues in quantum algorithm design, which is crucial for simulating complex molecular or material properties.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Real and generated samples are mixed during Double-DQN updates, supporting the search for low-error circuits with fewer entangling gates.

Figure 3 shows that transferred replay information improves both methods, but the improvement is substantially larger for GenQAS. For TensorRL-QAS, transfer of the uniform replay buffer reduces the steps to the first chemical-accuracy solution from 13623 to 9520, a 30.1% reduction. The transferred buffer also reduces the CNOT count from 13 to 9, a 30.8% reduction, but leaves the rotation count and circuit depth unchanged at 4 and 10, respectively. For GenQAS, transfer of the generative replay mechanism reduces the steps to chemical accuracy from 9053 to 660, corresponding to a 92.7% reduction.
